prompt: You hold four matches for one candle. Three are damp. How many flames do you get?
rationale: Only the dry match can light the candle. B mistakes the damp matches for successes.

prompt: A shelf holds six ration tins. You take away four. How many are in your hand?
rationale: You hold what you took, not what remains on the shelf. A answers the wrong question.

prompt: Rations last twelve days for four people. Two more arrive. How many days now?
rationale: Forty-eight person-days spread over six people gives eight. A wrongly halves for double the people.

prompt: A watch loses three minutes every hour. Set correctly at noon, what does it show at four?
rationale: Four hours times three lost minutes is twelve minutes behind: 3:48. C forgets the watch loses time at all.

prompt: A sign reads: if the tank is full, the light turns green. The light is green. Is the tank full?

options.text: Not necessarily, something else could cause it

rationale: The rule only says full implies green, not the reverse. B commits the classic error of affirming the consequent.

prompt: A candle burns down one centimetre every twenty minutes. It is eight centimetres tall. Roughly how long until it dies?
rationale: Eight centimetres at one per twenty minutes is a hundred sixty minutes, nearly three hours. D underestimates by forty minutes.

prompt: You find a fault in work that shipped last week. Nobody has noticed it yet.
rationale: Trades speed, standing, honesty, and cover, differently for each choice.

prompt: A friend on your team is behind, and it is starting to show in results only you can see.

options.text: Tell the lead what you see

rationale: Costs your time, the friendship, an ally, or the deadline, depending which you choose.

prompt: Two of three water cans are contaminated. You test one at random; it is clean. Chance the next one is also clean?
rationale: Only one clean can existed, and you already found it. The rest must be contaminated.

prompt: One well in a hundred is poisoned. A test that is ninety percent accurate comes back positive on yours. Is it poisoned?

options.text: Still probably clean, near one in twelve
No better than a coin flip

rationale: False positives from the ninety-nine clean wells outnumber true positives. A ignores how rare poisoning actually is.

prompt: Next in the sequence: 3, 7, 15, 31, __?
rationale: Each term doubles the last and adds one: 31 times two plus one is 63. B just doubles and forgets the plus one.

prompt: A courier sets out, travels six hours, rests one, then travels three more, ending the journey at six PM. When did he set out?
rationale: Six plus one plus three is ten hours before six PM, so eight AM. D miscounts the rest as travel time.

prompt: An offer arrives that changes your life. Your team ships in three weeks without you.
rationale: Costs money, goodwill, opportunity, or the offer itself, depending which you take.

prompt: You are asked to ship a feature you know is not ready, before anyone else can check it.

options.text: Ship it and flag the risk

rationale: Protects your name, the deadline, the team's trust, or your standing, never all four at once.
Each term is n times n plus one: five times six is thirty. A assumes a constant difference of eight.

prompt: A guard checks a gate every seven minutes, another every eleven. Both just checked together. Minutes until they align again?
rationale: The next joint check is the lowest common multiple of seven and eleven, which is seventy-seven. B guesses a sum instead.
Each term doubles the last and subtracts one: seventeen times two minus one is thirty-three. D is one short.

prompt: Your manager presents your work as theirs, to the people who decide your promotion.

options.text: Correct them in the room, now
Raise it with them privately after
Say nothing and build the record
Take it to their manager instead

rationale: Trades standing, the relationship, time, or safety, and none of the four is free.

prompt: You are good at work nobody notices. A worse fit for you would finally get you seen.
rationale: Trades recognition, mastery, patience, or a chance that may never come again.

prompt: Leaving now costs you nothing arranged. Staying costs you another year you already regret.
rationale: Each trades certainty against time differently. None of the four choices costs nothing.
